desc:
You may choose one substring of s (possibly of length 1, which changes nothing) and reverse it in place. Return the lexicographically smallest string you can obtain this way.

s = "dcba"
result = "abcd"

s = "abab"
result = "aabb"

s = "bcab"
result = "acbb"

In the last example reversing "bca" gives "acb" followed by the final b.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Trying every substring is O(n²) reversals of O(n) each. Think about which position should be the left end of the reversed substring.
The string can only improve at the first position i where some later letter is smaller than s[i]. Before that position every letter is already no larger than everything after it.
Start the reversal at that i. The end j must hold the smallest letter that occurs after i; try each such j and keep the smallest resulting string.
editorial: Let i be the first index with s[i] > min(s[i+1:]). If there is none, the string is already the best possible (every letter is at most all letters after it, so the string is sorted) and the answer is s. Otherwise the prefix s[:i] cannot be improved, and a reversal that starts at i brings a strictly smaller letter to position i, so the reversal must start exactly there.

The letter that lands on position i is s[j], and it must be the minimum letter m of s[i+1:]. Among all j > i with s[j] = m, build the candidate s[:i] + reverse(s[i:j+1]) + s[j+1:] and keep the smallest. There can be O(n) candidates of length O(n), so this is O(n²) in the worst case but with a tiny constant (slicing and comparison run at memory speed), which is fine for n ≤ 5,000.
